lead: In this week after Pentecost both readings speak of the Spirit. Paul tells the Galatians that Christ took our curse upon himself “so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.” Jesus warns that a soul emptied of evil but left empty is in danger: the house must be filled. The key words are blessing and the filled house.

set: Paul writes to the Churches of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey, probably in the mid-50s AD. After he left, other teachers had come and told the Gentile converts that to belong fully to God's people they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul answers that they received the Spirit not by works of the law but by believing the Gospel (3:2–5).

Today's verses form a chain of Old Testament texts: Genesis 12:3 and 18:18 (the blessing of the nations), Deuteronomy 27:26 (the curse), Habakkuk 2:4 (the righteous live by faith), Leviticus 18:5 (life by doing the law) and Deuteronomy 21:23 (one hanged on a tree). Paul argues as a trained Jewish teacher, from Scripture to Scripture.
str: vv. 7–9: the children of Abraham are those who believe; the nations are blessed in him.
vv. 10–12: the law, taken alone, cannot give life and leaves us under a curse.
vv. 13–14: Christ became a curse for us, so that the blessing and the Spirit come to all.
kw: Trust in God and his promise, as Abraham trusted (3:6; Genesis 15:6). For Paul faith is never idle: elsewhere in this letter he speaks of “faith working through love” (5:6).

The observances of the Mosaic law, such as circumcision and the food laws, when they are made the condition for belonging to God's people apart from Christ. Paul calls the law itself holy (Romans 7:12).
To buy out, to ransom, as a slave is bought out of slavery. Christ paid the price for us with his own life.
vv: so, you see, those who believe are the descendants of Abraham.
Abraham's true family is not only a matter of birth. Abraham himself believed God before he was circumcised (Romans 4:10–11).
Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law; for “The one who is righteous will live by faith.”
Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4. In Hebrew the word means faithfulness, steady trust in God. Paul hears in it the way of faith opened in Christ.
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us
Deuteronomy 21:23 says that one hanged on a tree is under God's curse. Paul sees the cross in that light: Jesus took the place of the cursed, so that we might receive the blessing.
so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
The promise made to Abraham reaches its goal at Pentecost: the gift of the Holy Spirit poured out on Jews and Gentiles alike.
ch: The Church teaches that justification has been merited for us by the Passion of Christ and is given through Baptism, the sacrament of faith (CCC 1992). Faith is the beginning of salvation, and the works that follow are themselves the fruit of grace, done in Christ and by his Spirit. Paul is not teaching that the law of Moses was evil or that God has rejected his people; the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). He teaches that in Christ the blessing promised to Abraham is opened to every nation.

r.h: The house swept and put in order
set: These verses close a controversy. Jesus has cast out a demon, and some say he does it by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons (11:14–15). He answers that he casts out demons “by the finger of God” (11:20), and that “Whoever is not with me is against me” (11:23). Then comes this short warning. Right after it a woman calls out a blessing on his mother, and Jesus answers: “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” (11:28). Matthew has the same saying (Matthew 12:43–45).
str: v. 24: the unclean spirit leaves, wanders, and decides to return.
v. 25: it finds the house swept and put in order.
v. 26: it brings seven worse spirits, and the last state is worse than the first.
kw: Rest, a place to settle. The evil spirit finds no rest in the desert and looks for a human heart to live in.
Clean and tidy, but in Matthew's version also “empty” (Matthew 12:44). Nothing new has come to live in the house.
The number of fullness in the Bible. The danger is not a small one but complete.
vv: it wanders through waterless regions looking for a resting place,
In the thinking of the time the desert was a place of evil spirits. The image is of a restless power that does not give up easily.
When it comes, it finds it swept and put in order.
Being cleaned is not enough. A life from which sin has been driven out must be filled with God, or it will be filled again by something worse.
and the last state of that person is worse than the first.
A warning against half-hearted conversion: to turn away from evil without turning towards Christ.
ch: The Church teaches that conversion is not only a first step at Baptism but a continual task for the whole Church and for each Christian, a “second conversion” that lasts a lifetime (CCC 1428). The context shows how the house is filled: by hearing the word of God and keeping it (11:28), and, in this season, by the Holy Spirit, who comes to dwell in those who belong to Christ.

study: Paul says that Christ became a curse for us. How does that change the way I look at my own sins and at the cross?
After I have confessed a sin, how do I fill the “swept house” with prayer, the word of God and good works?
